claim: The genetic control of anterior brain development is highly conserved throughout animals.
source: The genetic control of anterior brain development is highly conserved throughout animals.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by the subsequent citations and discussion of conserved gene regulatory networks.

claim: A conserved anterior gene regulatory network specifies the ancestral neuroendocrine center of animals and the apical organ of marine organisms.
source: For instance, a conserved anterior gene regulatory network specifies the ancestral neuroendocrine center of animals and the apical organ of marine organisms.
evidence: This statement is supported by the broader literature on anterior patterning genes, as indicated by the context of the abstract.

claim: Tc-foxQ2 is a key regulator of the anterior gene regulatory network of insects.
source: Here, we study the function of the Tc-foxQ2 forkhead transcription factor, a key regulator of the anterior gene regulatory network of insects.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the experimental work presented in the manuscript.

claim: Four distinct types of Tc-foxQ2 positive neural progenitor cells were characterized based on differential co-expression with Tc-six3/optix, Tc-six4, Tc-chx/vsx, Tc-nkx2.1/scro, Tc-ey, Tc-rx and Tc-fez1.
source: We characterized four distinct types of Tc-foxQ2 positive neural progenitor cells based on differential co-expression with Tc-six3/optix, Tc-six4, Tc-chx/vsx, Tc-nkx2.1/scro, Tc-ey, Tc-rx and Tc-fez1.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by the co-expression data shown in Figure 2.

claim: An enhancer trap line built by genome editing marked Tc-foxQ2 positive neurons.
source: An enhancer trap line built by genome editing marked Tc-foxQ2 positive neurons, which projected through the primary brain commissure and later through a subset of commissural fascicles.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by the generation and characterization of the foxQ2-5'-line shown in Figure 3.

claim: Tc-foxQ2 positive neurons projected through the primary brain commissure and later through a subset of commissural fascicles.
source: An enhancer trap line built by genome editing marked Tc-foxQ2 positive neurons, which projected through the primary brain commissure and later through a subset of commissural fascicles.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and shown in Figure 4.

claim: Tc-foxQ2 positive neurons eventually contributed to the central complex.
source: Eventually, they contributed to the central complex.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 5.

claim: In Tc-foxQ2 RNAi knock-down embryos the primary brain commissure did not split.
source: Strikingly, in Tc-foxQ2 RNAi knock-down embryos the primary brain commissure did not split and subsequent development of midline brain structures stalled.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and shown in Figure 7.

claim: Subsequent development of midline brain structures stalled in Tc-foxQ2 RNAi knock-down embryos.
source: Strikingly, in Tc-foxQ2 RNAi knock-down embryos the primary brain commissure did not split and subsequent development of midline brain structures stalled.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and shown in Figure 7.

claim: foxQ2 is a key regulator of brain midline structures, which distinguish the protocerebrum from segmental ganglia.
source: Our work establishes foxQ2 as a key regulator of brain midline structures, which distinguish the protocerebrum from segmental ganglia.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the experimental data presented.

claim: The central complex evolved by integrating neural cells from an ancestral anterior neuroendocrine center.
source: Unexpectedly, our data suggest that the central complex evolved by integrating neural cells from an ancestral anterior neuroendocrine center.
evidence: This is an evolutionary interpretation stated in the abstract based on the finding that foxQ2-positive cells contribute to the central complex.

claim: The brain is among the most complex organs found in animals.
source: The brain is among the most complex organs found in animals.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Many aspects of neural development are conserved in animals.
source: Many aspects of neural development are conserved in animals but compared to vertebrates, insects have a strongly reduced number of neural cells and the genes involved are usually present in single copy.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by comparative developmental biology literature.

claim: Compared to vertebrates, insects have a strongly reduced number of neural cells.
source: Many aspects of neural development are conserved in animals but compared to vertebrates, insects have a strongly reduced number of neural cells and the genes involved are usually present in single copy.
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on established knowledge in developmental neurobiology.

claim: In insects, the genes involved in neural development are usually present in single copy.
source: Many aspects of neural development are conserved in animals but compared to vertebrates, insects have a strongly reduced number of neural cells and the genes involved are usually present in single copy.
evidence: This is a statement about gene copy number in insects compared to vertebrates, based on genomic knowledge.

claim: Insects are very useful models to study the genetic control of neural development.
source: This has made insects very useful models to study the genetic control of neural development (Hartenstein and Stollewerk, 2015; Technau et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The insect central nervous system is composed of serially homologous segmental ganglia.
source: The insect central nervous system is composed of serially homologous segmental ganglia (Snodgrass, 1935; Weber, 1966).
evidence: This is a statement about insect neuroanatomy supported by citations.

claim: The protocerebrum is of different origin than segmental ganglia.
source: However, the anterior-most part of the brain, the protocerebrum, is of different origin.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by subsequent citations.

claim: The protocerebrum stems from an anterior non-segmental tissue dating back to the last common bilaterian ancestor.
source: It stems from an anterior non-segmental tissue dating back to the last common bilaterian ancestor (Arendt et al., 2008; Rempel, 1975; Scholtz and Edgecombe, 2006; Snodgrass, 1935; Strausfeld, 2012; Weber, 1966).
evidence: This is an evolutionary statement supported by multiple citations.

claim: A number of neural patterning genes are expressed in the anterior brain anlagen but not in the trunk of animals from vertebrates to insects.
source: Accordingly, a number of neural patterning genes are expressed in the anterior brain anlagen but not in the trunk of animals from vertebrates to insects (Acampora et al., 1998; Arendt and Nübler-Jung, 1996; Arendt et al., 2008; Gehring, 1996; Hirth et al., 1995; Hirth et al., 2003; Lowe et al., 2003; Posnien et al., 2011b; Quiring et al., 1994; Sinigaglia et al., 2013; Steinmetz et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to comparative gene expression studies.

claim: A number of transcription factors that confer spatial identity to trunk neuroblasts are expressed in a quite modified way or not at all in the protocerebral neuroectoderm.
source: Conversely, a number of transcription factors that confer spatial identity to trunk neuroblasts (NBs) are expressed in a quite modified way or not at all in the protocerebral neuroectoderm (Urbach and Technau, 2003a; Urbach and Technau, 2003b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on neuroblast specification.

claim: The protocerebrum contains unique structures like the optic lobes and the mushroom bodies.
source: The former contains unique structures like the optic lobes, the mushroom bodies and is marked by a set of midline-spanning neuropils, the central complex (CX) (El Jundi and Heinze, 2016; Pfeiffer and Homberg, 2014; Snodgrass, 1935; Strausfeld, 2012; Weber, 1966).
evidence: This is a statement about protocerebral anatomy supported by citations.

claim: The protocerebrum is marked by a set of midline-spanning neuropils, the central complex.
source: The former contains unique structures like the optic lobes, the mushroom bodies and is marked by a set of midline-spanning neuropils, the central complex (CX) (El Jundi and Heinze, 2016; Pfeiffer and Homberg, 2014; Snodgrass, 1935; Strausfeld, 2012; Weber, 1966).
evidence: This is a statement about protocerebral anatomy supported by citations.

claim: Fascicle switching occurs in the commissure of the brain but not the ventral nerve cord.
source: Further, a process called fascicle switching occurs in the commissure of the brain but not the ventral nerve cord.
evidence: This is a statement about a developmental process specific to the brain.

claim: In fascicle switching, some neurites leave their commissural fascicle (de-fasciculation) and join another commissural fascicle (re-fasciculation).
source: In that process, some neurites leave their commissural fascicle (de-fasciculation) and join another commissural fascicle (re-fasciculation).
evidence: This is a description of the fascicle switching process.

claim: Fascicle switching leads to the typical X-shaped chiasmata (decussations) of the central body.
source: Fascicle switching leads to the typical X-shaped chiasmata (decussations) of the central body and is essential for CX development (Boyan et al., 2008; Boyan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on central complex development.

claim: Fascicle switching is essential for CX development.
source: Fascicle switching leads to the typical X-shaped chiasmata (decussations) of the central body and is essential for CX development (Boyan et al., 2008; Boyan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on central complex development.

claim: A molecular subdivision within the protocerebrum was found where an anterior optix/six3 positive region distinguishes an ancestral neuroendocrine center of animals from a more posterior otd/otx positive region.
source: Recently, a molecular subdivision within the protocerebrum was found where an anterior optix/six3 positive region distinguishes an ancestral neuroendocrine center of animals from a more posterior otd/otx positive region (Kittelmann et al., 2013; Steinmetz et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The components and some of their interactions of the anterior gene regulatory network (aGRN) including six3 and foxQ2 are conserved within animals.
source: The components and some of their interactions of the anterior gene regulatory network (aGRN) including six3 and foxQ2 are conserved within animals (Hunnekuhl and Akam, 2014; Kitzmann et al., 2017; Lowe et al., 2003; Marlow et al., 2013; Range and Wei, 2016; Sinigaglia et al., 2013; Wei et al., 2009; Yaguchi et al., 2008; Yaguchi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to comparative studies.

claim: The anterior neural region marked by the aGRN gives rise to the apical organ of marine animals including ciliated cells like the apical tuft.
source: Apart from marking neuroendocrine cells throughout animal clades, this neural region gives rise to the apical organ of marine animals including ciliated cells like the apical tuft (Dunn et al., 2007; Marlow et al., 2013; Santagata et al., 2012; Sinigaglia et al., 2013; Wei et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on marine larvae development.

claim: The anterior brain of bilaterians evolved by the fusion of an ancestral apical brain with an ancestral blastoporal brain located at the opposite pole of the animal.
source: It was proposed that the anterior brain of bilaterians evolved by the fusion of an ancestral apical brain with an ancestral blastoporal brain located at the opposite pole of the animal (Tosches and Arendt, 2013).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the cited work.

claim: The ancestral apical brain contained cells for neuroendocrine control and non-visual photoreception and was patterned by the expression of six3 and rx.
source: In this model, the ancestral apical brain contained cells for neuroendocrine control and non-visual photoreception and was patterned by the expression of six3 and rx.
evidence: This is part of the chimeric brain hypothesis described in the cited work.

claim: Based on recent data, foxQ2 adds to the list of apical markers.
source: Based on recent data, foxQ2 adds to this list of apical markers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression pattern and function of foxQ2.

claim: The blastoporal nervous system was located at the opposite pole of the animal, performed a sensory contractile function and was marked by the expression of nk2.1, Pax6 and other genes.
source: The blastoporal nervous system, in contrast, was located at the opposite pole of the animal, performed a sensory contractile function and was marked by the expression of nk2.1, Pax6 and other genes.
evidence: This is part of the chimeric brain hypothesis described in the cited work.

claim: The anterior part of the blastoporal system fused with the apical brain to form an evolutionary 'chimera' forming the anterior brain of extant bilaterians.
source: Starting from this ancestral condition, the anterior part of the blastoporal system fused with the apical brain to form an evolutionary 'chimera' forming the anterior brain of extant bilaterians.
evidence: This is part of the chimeric brain hypothesis described in the cited work.

claim: Anterior and tuberal hypothalamus and the retina of vertebrates were proposed to be of chimeric origin.
source: For instance anterior and tuberal hypothalamus and the retina of vertebrates were proposed to be of chimeric origin (Tosches and Arendt, 2013).
evidence: This is a specific example from the chimeric brain hypothesis.

claim: It has remained unclear to which non-neuroendocrine structures the apical region might contribute in arthropods, which do not have an apical organ.
source: However, it has remained unclear to which non-neuroendocrine structures the apical region might contribute in arthropods, which do not have an apical organ (Hunnekuhl and Akam, 2014; Marlow et al., 2014).
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: The identity of the neural parts representing the hypothetical chimeric anterior brain has remained enigmatic in insects.
source: Further, the identity of the neural parts representing the hypothetical chimeric anterior brain has remained enigmatic in insects.
evidence: This identifies another gap in knowledge.

claim: Tribolium castaneum represents a more ancestral situation of anterior neuroectoderm development than Drosophila.
source: First, it represents a more ancestral situation of anterior neuroectoderm development.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent description of differences in blastodermal geometry.

claim: In Tribolium and most other insects including the basal hemimetabolan insects, the brain neuroectoderm derives from a subterminal ventral blastodermal region.
source: In Tribolium and most other insects including the basal hemimetabolan insects, the brain neuroectoderm derives from a subterminal ventral blastodermal region rather than from the anterior dorsal blastoderm as found in Drosophila.
evidence: This is a comparative statement about embryonic development.

claim: In Drosophila, the brain neuroectoderm derives from the anterior dorsal blastoderm.
source: In Tribolium and most other insects including the basal hemimetabolan insects, the brain neuroectoderm derives from a subterminal ventral blastodermal region rather than from the anterior dorsal blastoderm as found in Drosophila.
evidence: This is a comparative statement about embryonic development.

claim: The difference in blastodermal geometry between Tribolium and Drosophila results in divergent genetic regulation.
source: This difference in blastodermal geometry results in divergent genetic regulation (Ansari et al., 2018; Fu et al., 2012; Kittelmann et al., 2013; Nunes da Fonseca et al., 2008; Posnien et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to comparative developmental studies.

claim: With respect to transgenesis, misexpression, genome editing, efficient genome wide RNAi screening and other tools for analysis of gene function, Tribolium is a genetic model insect second only to Drosophila.
source: With respect to transgenesis, misexpression, genome editing, efficient genome wide RNAi screening and other tools for analysis of gene function, Tribolium is a genetic model insect second only to Drosophila (Berghammer et al., 1999; Bucher et al., 2002; Dönitz et al., 2018; Gilles et al., 2015; Schinko et al., 2010; Schmitt-Engel et al., 2015; Tomoyasu and Denell, 2004; Trauner et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to methodological papers.

claim: Tc-foxQ2 is exclusively expressed in the region patterned by the aGRN.
source: In this work we examined the role of the forkhead transcription factor Tc-foxQ2 in brain development because this gene is exclusively expressed in the region patterned by the aGRN (Kitzmann et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: foxQ2 is a highly conserved anterior patterning gene.
source: Further, it is a highly conserved anterior patterning gene.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent citations to studies in various organisms.

claim: Orthologs of foxQ2 are involved in anterior-most specification of neural cells in many clades of bilaterians and in cnidarians.
source: Orthologs of foxQ2 are involved in anterior-most specification of neural cells in many clades of bilaterians and in cnidarians (Darras et al., 2011; Fritzenwanker et al., 2014; Hunnekuhl and Akam, 2014; Leclère et al., 2016; Marlow et al., 2013; Range and Wei, 2016; Range and Wei, 2016; Sinigaglia et al., 2013; Wei et al., 2009; Yaguchi et al., 2008; Yaguchi et al., 2010; Yu et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to comparative studies.

claim: foxQ2 was lost from the genome in amphibians and mammals.
source: A notable exception are amphibians and mammals, where the gene was lost from the genome (Mazet et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Anterior expression of foxQ2 orthologs was described in Drosophila (fd102C, CG11152) and Strigamia maritima, a myriapod.
source: In arthropods, anterior expression of foxQ2 orthologs was described in Drosophila (fd102C, CG11152) and Strigamia maritima, a myriapod (Hunnekuhl and Akam, 2014; Lee and Frasch, 2004) correlating with the location of neuroendocrine cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to expression studies.

claim: The anterior expression of foxQ2 orthologs in arthropods correlates with the location of neuroendocrine cells.
source: In arthropods, anterior expression of foxQ2 orthologs was described in Drosophila (fd102C, CG11152) and Strigamia maritima, a myriapod (Hunnekuhl and Akam, 2014; Lee and Frasch, 2004) correlating with the location of neuroendocrine cells.
evidence: This is an observation from the cited studies.

claim: Tc-foxQ2 acts together with six3/optix upstream in the aGRN to build the labrum.
source: Recently, we have shown an upstream role of Tc-foxQ2 in anterior head epidermis patterning in Tribolium where it acts together with six3/optix upstream in the aGRN to build the labrum (Kitzmann et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: An effect on embryonic CX development was noted after Tc-foxQ2 knock-down.
source: Intriguingly, an effect on embryonic CX development was noted as well.
evidence: This refers to observations from previous work.

claim: The two CX neuropils protocerebral bridge (PB) and central body (CB) form partially during embryogenesis in Tribolium and some other holometabolan taxa.
source: The two CX neuropils protocerebral bridge (PB) and central body (CB) form partially during embryogenesis in Tribolium and some other holometabolan taxa (Koniszewski et al., 2016; Panov, 1959; Wegerhoff and Breidbach, 1992) while in Drosophila the first functional CX neuropil appears during pupation.
evidence: This is a comparative statement about CX development supported by citations.

claim: In Drosophila the first functional CX neuropil appears during pupation.
source: The two CX neuropils protocerebral bridge (PB) and central body (CB) form partially during embryogenesis in Tribolium and some other holometabolan taxa (Koniszewski et al., 2016; Panov, 1959; Wegerhoff and Breidbach, 1992) while in Drosophila the first functional CX neuropil appears during pupation.
evidence: This is a comparative statement about CX development.

claim: In the ancestral situation represented by the hemimetabolan insect Schistocerca gregaria, the entire brain forms during embryogenesis.
source: In the ancestral situation represented for instance by the hemimetabolan insect Schistocerca gregaria, the entire brain forms during embryogenesis (Boyan et al., 2017; Koniszewski et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: In Tribolium larvae, the CB neuropil forms a simple bar crossing the midline.
source: In Tribolium larvae, the CB neuropil forms a simple bar crossing the midline.
evidence: This is a description of larval brain anatomy.

claim: The larval CB position prefigures the one of the adult CB but it still lacks columnar structure and subdivision into upper and lower divisions (fan-shaped and ellipsoid body, respectively).
source: Its position prefigures the one of the adult CB but it still lacks columnar structure and subdivision into upper and lower divisions (fan-shaped and ellipsoid body, respectively) (Koniszewski et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: A modification of the shape of the larval CB was observed after RNAi knock-down of Tc-foxQ2.
source: A modification of the shape of the larval CB was observes after RNAi knock-down of Tc-foxQ2 but apart from that, functional data on the neural function of foxQ2 had been missing in any protostome.
evidence: This refers to previous observations.

claim: Functional data on the neural function of foxQ2 had been missing in any protostome prior to this study.
source: A modification of the shape of the larval CB was observes after RNAi knock-down of Tc-foxQ2 but apart from that, functional data on the neural function of foxQ2 had been missing in any protostome.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: Tc-foxQ2 was continuously expressed in anterior median cell clusters from neural progenitors to postmitotic neurons of the late embryonic, larval and adult brains.
source: We found that Tc-foxQ2 was continuously expressed in anterior median cell clusters from neural progenitors to postmitotic neurons of the late embryonic, larval and adult brains.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the expression data shown in Figures 1-3.

claim: Tc-foxQ2 positive neurons project through the primary brain commissure and later into the upper unit of the central body (fan-shaped body).
source: Further, we generated genetic neural imaging lines and found that Tc-foxQ2 positive neurons project through the primary brain commissure and later into the upper unit of the central body (fan-shaped body).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Tc-foxQ2 RNAi-knock-down embryos failed to develop brain midline structures.
source: Tc-foxQ2 RNAi-knock-down embryos failed to develop brain midline structures: The primary brain commissure did form but failed to split into the large number of protocerebral commissures.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7.

claim: The primary brain commissure formed in Tc-foxQ2 RNAi-knock-down embryos but failed to split into the large number of protocerebral commissures.
source: Tc-foxQ2 RNAi-knock-down embryos failed to develop brain midline structures: The primary brain commissure did form but failed to split into the large number of protocerebral commissures.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7.

claim: CB formation was abolished in Tc-foxQ2 RNAi-knock-down embryos.
source: Consequently, the CB formation was abolished.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7.

claim: Tc-foxQ2 is one of the key factors of embryonic brain development contributing to the different development of the protocerebrum versus segmental ganglia.
source: These results identify Tc-foxQ2 as one of the key factors of embryonic brain development contributing to the different development of the protocerebrum versus segmental ganglia.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the experimental data.

claim: Cells patterned by the aGRN contribute to the CX, a unique protocerebral brain structure.
source: Unexpectedly, our results show that cells patterned by the aGRN contribute to the CX, a unique protocerebral brain structure.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the finding that Tc-foxQ2 positive cells contribute to the CX.

claim: The insect CX evolved by integrating cells from the ancestral anterior-most neuroectoderm, which gives rise to the apical organ including the apical tuft in marine animals.
source: Apparently, the insect CX evolved by integrating cells from the ancestral anterior-most neuroectoderm, which gives rise to the apical organ including the apical tuft in marine animals.
evidence: This is an evolutionary interpretation stated in the Results section.

claim: Tc-foxQ2 is expressed in the anterior neuroectoderm from earliest stages onwards indicating a role in the specification of neuroblasts.
source: In the embryo, Tc-foxQ2 is expressed in the anterior neuroectoderm from earliest stages onwards indicating a role in the specification of neuroblasts (Kitzmann et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: An intronic probe of Tc-asense (Tc-ase) was used as marker for NPCs, which could be either NBs, intermediate neural progenitors (INPs) of type II NBs or ganglion mother cells (GMCs).
source: To that end we generated an antibody specific for the Tc-FoxQ2 protein (see Materials and methods and Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and used an intronic probe of Tc-asense (Tc-ase) as marker for NPCs, which could be either NBs, intermediate neural progenitors (INPs) of type II NBs or ganglion mother cells (GMCs) (Boone and Doe, 2008; Bowman et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes the methodology used, supported by citations.

claim: Tc-ase has been shown to be a marker for NBs in Tribolium.
source: It should be noted that the Tc-ase has been shown to be a marker for NBs in Tribolium (Wheeler et al., 2003) but that its expression in INPs or GMCs is assumed by analogy from Drosophila.
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The expression of Tc-ase in INPs or GMCs in Tribolium is assumed by analogy from Drosophila.
source: It should be noted that the Tc-ase has been shown to be a marker for NBs in Tribolium (Wheeler et al., 2003) but that its expression in INPs or GMCs is assumed by analogy from Drosophila.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge from Drosophila.

claim: The first protocerebral NPCs delaminate at NS4.
source: The first protocerebral NPCs delaminate at NS4.
evidence: This is a statement about the timing of NPC delamination.

claim: The first Tc-FoxQ2+ NPCs emerge at NS8.
source: The first Tc-FoxQ2+ NPCs, however, emerge at NS8.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1.

claim: At NS8, about 15 Tc-FoxQ2+/Tc-ase+ cells were identified forming a large anterior group, a small median group and a single lateral cell.
source: Here, about 15 Tc-FoxQ2+/Tc-ase+ cells were identified (n = 6; Figure 1A; Supplementary file 1-table 1) forming a large anterior group (blue and green in Figure 1A''), a small median group (gray) and a single lateral cell (orange).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: At NS11, the number of Tc-FoxQ2+/Tc-ase+ cells had decreased to 9–12 cells.
source: At NS11, the number had decreased to 9–12 cells expressing both markers (n = 6; Figure 1B; Supplementary file 1-table 1) while at least 5–7 cells were observed at stage 14 (n = 6; Figure 1C; Supplementary file 1-table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: At stage 14, at least 5–7 Tc-FoxQ2+/Tc-ase+ cells were observed.
source: At NS11, the number had decreased to 9–12 cells expressing both markers (n = 6; Figure 1B; Supplementary file 1-table 1) while at least 5–7 cells were observed at stage 14 (n = 6; Figure 1C; Supplementary file 1-table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The reduction in Tc-FoxQ2+/Tc-ase+ cell number could be due to Tc-ase expression ceasing once NBs enter quiescence.
source: This reduction could have several reasons: Tc-ase expression may cease once NBs enter quiescence like in Drosophila (Lai and Doe, 2014) or Tc-foxQ2 expression may become repressed in a subset of NPCs.
evidence: This is a speculation about the cause of the observed reduction, supported by a citation.

claim: The reduction in Tc-FoxQ2+/Tc-ase+ cell number could be due to Tc-foxQ2 expression becoming repressed in a subset of NPCs.
source: This reduction could have several reasons: Tc-ase expression may cease once NBs enter quiescence like in Drosophila (Lai and Doe, 2014) or Tc-foxQ2 expression may become repressed in a subset of NPCs.
evidence: This is a speculation about the cause of the observed reduction.

claim: If the anterior group contained type II NBs, the double positive cells would be INPs or GMCs, which express asense while type II NBs themselves do not.
source: Alternatively, if the anterior group contained type II NBs, the double positive cells would be INPs or GMCs, which based on Drosophila knowledge express asense while type II NBs themselves do not (Boone and Doe, 2008; Bowman et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a speculation based on knowledge from Drosophila, supported by citations.

claim: Markers for unequivocally distinguishing NBs, INPs and GMCs remain to be established in Tribolium.
source: Unfortunately, markers for unequivocally distinguishing NBs, INPs and GMCs remain to be established in Tribolium.
evidence: This identifies a limitation in the current methodology.

claim: Four different molecular types of Tc-FoxQ2+ NPCs were found that correlated with positional differences.
source: We found four different molecular types that correlated with positional differences (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The first type (P-fox-am) was the largest group and was located anterior median in the neuroectoderm, showing co-expression of Tc-foxQ2 with Tc-six3 (optix), Tc-six4 and later Tc-chx (vsx).
source: The first type (No1 in Figure 2I') was the largest group and was located anterior median in the neuroectoderm. This type showed co-expression of Tc-foxQ2 with Tc-six3 (optix), Tc-six4 and later Tc-chx (vsx). We call these cells the P-fox-am group of cells (P stands for protocerebral according to Drosophila nomenclature [Younossi-Hartenstein et al., 1996]).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The second type (P-fox-amp) was located posteriorly adjacent to P-fox-am and showed additional expression of Tc-scro (nkx2.1), Tc-earmuff (fez1) and in one of the cells also Tc-eyeless (Pax6).
source: The second type (P-fox-amp) was located posteriorly adjacent and was similar to the P-fox-am but showed additional expression of Tc-scro (nkx2.1), Tc-earmuff (fez1) and in one of the cells also Tc-eyeless (Pax6) (No2 in Figure 2I').
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: A third type (P-fox-l) consisted of one lateral NPC, which co-expressed Tc-six3 with Tc-earmuff, Tc-rx and Tc-eyeless.
source: A third type consisted of one lateral NPC, which co-expressed Tc-six3 with Tc-earmuff, Tc-rx and Tc-eyeless (No3 in Figure 2I').
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The fourth type (P-fox-v) showed only co-expression of Tc-foxQ2 and Tc-scro and was located at a ventral position adjacent to the stomodeum.
source: The fourth type showed only co-expression of Tc-foxQ2 and Tc-scro (No4 in Figure 2I') and was located at a ventral position adjacent to the stomodeum (P-fox-v).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

source: A second glia sheet appeared to surround the medial-most cells marked with lower levels of EGFP (open arrowhead in Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

source: At NS15 approximately 15–20 cells were marked (n = 4; Supplementary file 1-table 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The projections of the anterior-lateral-foxQ2-lineage joined the established Tc-foxQ2 positive neurites at a lateral position.
source: They formed a column-like cluster lateral to the anterior-median-foxQ2-cluster (orange arrowheads in Figure 5B,D) and their projections joined the established Tc-foxQ2 positive neurites at a lateral position (white arrows in Figure 5B,D).

source: Because this cluster contained only one NB and all cells were within one glia sheath (orange arrowhead in Figure 4—figure supplement 1) we hypothesize that they form one neural lineage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed data.

source: By tracing back this lineage to the embryonic ectoderm we found that it most likely derived from the P-fox-l NPC (Figure 2I').
